What will you build?

Describe a medical device and what it must detect. designs the chip inside it.

A bedside monitor that warns when a heartbeat turns irregular.
Join waitlist

Scroll to watch a run

  1. Thousands of designs.

    From one description, AI scientists propose thousands of candidate chips. Each one is a small AI model with its own shape.

  2. Fine-tuned at once.

    Every candidate learns in the same batch. The pale blue wave is training passing through them.

  3. Thousands, then one.

    The best candidate becomes the chip. Sensor signals flow in, through the small fine-tuned model, and a prediction flows out.

  4. The model, as logic gates.

    Up close, the model is wired into gates, its weights built into the circuit. Then it is checked against the model.

    2,330One small heart-rhythm detector became 2,330 logic gatesEarly feasibility test, not yet clinical
    3,880 of 3,880Test windows where the circuit matched its model, bit for bitEarly feasibility test, not yet clinical

  5. Smaller, then smaller.

    The scientists keep cutting while the chip still does its job. A smaller chip:

    • uses less power
    • lasts longer on a battery
    • costs less
    • fits inside the device

  6. One chip per device.

    Every device gets its own chip, shaped for its job. Click any chip to look closer. Illustration

RunHeart-rhythm monitorIllustration
  1. Description read: irregular heartbeat, one chest sensor
  2. Scientists proposed 4,096 candidate designs
  3. Training data, from one of:Public datasetYour own dataSimulated, assumptions stated
  4. Fine-tuning 4,096 candidates at once
  5. Candidates under the good-enough line
  6. Best candidate compiled into logic gates
  7. Circuit checked against its model
  8. Smallest chip that does the job, kept
  9. Chip returned for the device

So many kinds of device.

Each kind is its own detection problem, and each could use a chip made for it.
